title: Mridangam (South Indian barrel drum)
summary: The mridangam is the double-headed drum of South Indian classical music. Its body is turned from a single block of jackfruit wood and the two heads are laced together with leather straps. The right head carries a permanent black circle of paste and rings with a clear pitch; the left head is dressed with a little paste before playing and speaks in a deep bass.
howToPlay: Four spoken syllables sit on the drum: Thom is the bass of the left head, Din the ringing stroke of the right head, Ki a light touch at the centre of the black circle and Ta a flat stroke near the rim.
A ring closes on a place when its syllable is due. Strike it as the ring meets the skin.
Say the syllables aloud as you play, as students do when learning the rhythm cycles.
rules: A stroke on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strokes cost points.
Each pattern is played twice through.
Patterns are simplified teaching cycles in the style of South Indian rhythm, not transcriptions.
heritageNote: In a concert the mridangam supports the singer or the violin and answers with patterns of rhythm syllables. The syllables are the same ones a player speaks aloud when learning.
